text:
Richard Stallman was born in New York City in 1953 to a Jewish family. He developed an early interest in computers and worked at IBM during high school. At Harvard, he excelled in mathematics and physics, later becoming a researcher at MIT's Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. There, he became a prominent figure in the hacker community, known as RMS, and contributed to key software projects like Emacs and GCC.
In the late 1970s, Stallman became increasingly critical of proprietary software and its restrictive licensing, which he viewed as unethical and antithetical to user freedom. This led to the founding of the Free Software Foundation (FSF) in 1983, with the goal of creating a free operating system, GNU, compatible with Unix. He championed the concept of "copyleft," ensuring that free software could be freely modified and shared.
Stallman's work on the GNU project included developing essential tools such as the Emacs text editor, GCC compiler, and GNU Debugger. The project was completed in parts, with the kernel eventually provided by Linus Torvalds' Linux project, leading to the creation of GNU/Linux. Stallman has consistently advocated for software freedom, opposing software patents, digital rights management (DRM), and surveillance, and promoting open access to information.
He has also been a vocal critic of government and corporate surveillance, and has spoken out against software that limits user rights. Stallman's activism includes efforts to promote free software in education, such as persuading Indian state schools to switch from proprietary to free software. He has also supported initiatives like GNUPedia, which later evolved into Wikipedia.
In 1999, he advocated for a free online encyclopedia, and in 2006, he promoted a reduced copyright model, suggesting a 10-year limit and a system for fair distribution of author support. He has been a strong proponent of using free software in all aspects of computing, from operating systems to personal devices, and has maintained a personal commitment to using only free software.
Stallman has faced controversy, including criticism over his past writings on child pornography and pedophilia, which he later retracted and apologized for. In 2019, he resigned from MIT and the FSF over a misunderstanding regarding MIT's ties to Jeffrey Epstein, but returned to the FSF board in 2021. He continues to be a central figure in the free software movement, advocating for user freedom, transparency, and ethical software development.
